    Labels

    labels.Rmd

    Labels put the number — or the site name — behind each symbol. One parameter, marker_labels, controls both what a label says and when it appears:

    library(quickmap)                          # load the quickmap library
quickmap(
  "tubes_wandsworth.csv",
  boroughs      = "Wandsworth",
  marker_labels = TRUE                     # values appear on hover
)

    1. The five modes

    marker_labels = What appears When
    FALSE (default) nothing —
    TRUE the site’s value on hover
    "values_on" the site’s value always shown
    "labels" the site’s name on hover
    "labels_on" the site’s name always shown

    2. Always-visible values

    For a map whose reader shouldn’t have to hover — a report screenshot, a public page — show the values permanently:

    quickmap(
  "tubes_wandsworth.csv",
  boroughs      = "Wandsworth",
  marker_labels = "values_on"              # NEW: values always shown
)

    3. Site names instead of values

    Where a label says a name, the name comes from the data — no extra parameter, just the right column:

    quickmap(
  list("tubes_wandsworth_labelled.csv", # tubes WITH a Label column
       "schools_wandsworth.csv"),                  # schools (School column)
  boroughs      = "Wandsworth",
  marker_labels = "labels"                 # NEW: names on hover
)

    4. How label content is chosen

    Per layer, by its columns (duck typing):

    The layer has… "labels" shows
    a School column the school’s name
    a Label column the label text
    neither the site’s value (with a warning)
    • Gotcha: in a CSV with a Label column, rows whose label cell is empty are dropped from the map entirely — fill or remove empty label cells.
    • Mixed maps mix naturally: in the example above the tubes show their labels and the schools their names, each layer from its own column.

    Because the choice is made per layer, one setting can do two jobs. marker_labels = "values_on" on a map of tubes and schools gives every tube its value and every school its name — even if the tube file also has a Label column, since a School column always wins. Values read 28 µg/m³.

    5. Size and background

    Labels are the smallest text on a map, matched to the smallest text in the legend, and they scale with a static export automatically — a 4000-pixel image gets 4000-pixel-sized labels without being asked.

    Two theme keys adjust them:

    map:
  label_scale: 1           # multiplier: 2 is twice the legend's small text
  label_background: true   # the translucent plate behind each label

    label_background: false removes the plate, leaving the text alone on the map. The plate buys legibility over busy tiles and costs clutter where labels are dense — worth turning off on a print map.

    label_scale is a trade, not a free win: bigger labels collide sooner. On a crowded borough map, labels twice this size begin to overlap in the built-up centre, and much beyond that they cover the map. If you need larger text on paper, print the image bigger before raising this — the same file across A3 is twice the point size for nothing.

    6. Reference layers get a key, not labels

    A layer with no values — schools are the usual case — has no place on the colour ramp, so its symbol is explained in the banner instead. Where such a layer has a Level column, its categories appear at the end of the banner as small marks in their own colours (“✕ Primary ✕ Secondary”).

    That key is what lets the map labels drop the words every school shares. “Abbotsbury Primary School” can be labelled “Abbotsbury” once the banner has said what a blue cross means.
